newsitem.title: SUDAN: Khartoum says door open to political solution.
newsitem.headline: Khartoum says door open to political solution.

text.p: The Sudanese vice president said on Thursday that the door was open for a political solution to the conflict in eastern Sudan but the Sudanese army would continue to fight as long as it was attacked.

"All doors to solutions are open according to us. We are still looking for a political solution, because a political solution is a complete solution," Lieutenant-General al-Zubeir Mohammad Saleh told Reuters.
"But if someone attacks us or any part of our land, there is no choice but to...fight," he added.
Sudan says neighbouring Ethiopia and Eritrea have invaded eastern Sudan but the Sudanese opposition in exile say they are responsible for the attacks, without foreign help.

Saleh did not say what kind of talks or political solution he envisaged but Khartoum has made overtures in the past to both the northern Arab opposition and the Sudan People's Liberation Army (SPLA), which has been fighting in the south since 1983.
The Islamist government has invited the SPLA to join other southern groups in signing a national charter for peace. The SPLA says the charter is a sell-out.
The northern opposition says the Islamist military government is not seriously interested in sharing power or restoring the democratic system it destroyed in 1989.
The opposition National Democratic Alliance said in a statement on Thursday that it had to take up arms because the Sudanese government had closed the doors to peaceful change.
"It has abolished intellectual, party and political pluralism, freedom of thought and expression, and it has set up phoney legislative institutions," it added.
On Thursday Sudanese Information Minister Brigadier al-Tayeb Ibrahim Khair also said that Khartoum was asking southern neighbour Uganda to stop a third front opening in the south.

"The forces of (SPLA leader) John Garang are in the south of Sudan at the Ugandan border. There is an aim to open a third front, especially with American support for Ethiopia, Eritrea and Uganda," the minister told a briefing.
"We do not rule out that there will be a new front in this region and we are asking the Ugandan government to stop this."
Sudan has in the past said Uganda and Ethiopia have made cross-border raids in support of the SPLA. Uganda and Ethiopia says Khartoum supports rebels fighting them.

Asked which countries he thought were now fighting, Saleh said: "The attacks on Sudan...are from the Ethiopian border and Eritrea. Some Ethiopian forces entered Sudan and there are some of the forces of Garang."
Saleh has just returned from Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Syria and Qatar trying to muster support for his government.
He said that in Egypt, where the opposition in exile has a large political presence, he told President Hosni Mubarak that the aim of the attacks was to dismember Sudan.
"It is the same plan and same aim which happened in the Horn of Africa," he added.
Saleh spoke to Reuters after addressing a rally in central Khartoum to mark the arrival of a convoy of food from northern Sudan en route to the southern front.
Hundreds of men and women packed the courtyard of a local government building, waving axes and copies of the Koran in the air as musicians played war songs on electric guitars.
Speakers attacked opposition leader Sadeq al-Mahdi, who fled Khartoum for exile last month. "Mahdi is cooperating with the enemies of Sudan to kill the Sudanese people," said one.
